gloss_terse: To deliver, rescue, snatch away; Niphal: escape, be delivered; Piel: strip, plunder; Hifil: save from danger or enemies
gloss_readable: At its Hifil core, natsal is the Hebrew Bible's premier rescue verb — God snatching Israel from Egypt's hand, a shepherd pulling a lamb from the lion's jaws, a warrior delivering the oppressed. Arabic splits the range cleanly: anjadha for rescue, intaza'a for snatching away, and salaba for plundering — three distinct roots confirming real semantic fractures. The Niphal reflexive adds escape and self-deliverance, while the rare Piel transforms the verb entirely into its opposite: stripping and plundering the defeated. One Hithpael occurrence extends the root to stripping off one's own ornaments in grief.

senses.1: The dominant Hifil causative: to deliver, rescue, or save someone from danger, enemies, or death. At 188 occurrences this is natsal's gravitational center — from the Passover deliverance (Exod 12:27) to David's praise of divine rescue (2 Sam 22:1). Arabic anjadha/najja, Spanish librar, and Korean geonjida all converge on forcible extraction from peril.
senses.2: The Niphal passive-reflexive: to be delivered, escape, or deliver oneself. Fifteen occurrences including Jacob's deliverance at Peniel (Gen 32:30) and the psalmist's plea from the mire (Ps 69:14). Arabic yanju ('to escape'), Korean guwon-batda ('receive salvation'), and Deut 23:15's runaway-slave law confirm both passive and reflexive nuance.
senses.3: A distinct Hifil nuance of snatching away or forcibly removing possessions — not rescue but seizure. God 'snatched away' Laban's livestock for Jacob (Gen 31:9, 16) and Hosea warns of divine repossession (Hos 2:9). Arabic intaza'a ('to wrench away') and Hindi chhina ('snatched') use roots entirely distinct from rescue vocabulary.
senses.4: The Piel intensive: to strip, plunder, or despoil — the verb's semantic opposite. Three occurrences: Israel plundered the Egyptians (Exod 3:22, 12:36) and Jehoshaphat's army stripped fallen Moabites (2 Chr 20:25). Arabic salaba ('to plunder') and Korean ppae-atda ('seized') confirm a wholesale inversion from deliverance to dispossession.
senses.5: Prophetic imagery of 'a brand plucked from the fire' — rescue at the last moment before annihilation. Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2 form a vivid metaphor of narrow escape from total destruction. Spanish arrebatado ('snatched away') marks the desperate-rescue intensity beyond ordinary deliverance.
senses.6: A singular Hithpael reflexive at Exod 33:6: Israel 'stripped themselves of' their ornaments at Horeb after the golden calf judgment. Spanish se despojaron and French depouilla confirm self-directed removal of adornment — semantically closer to Piel stripping but reflexive and penitential rather than predatory.

gloss_terse: To lie down, recline, sleep; euphemism for sexual intercourse; Hifil: lay someone down; also: pour out (liquid)
gloss_readable: Shakab is the Hebrew Bible's universal posture verb for the horizontal — lying down to sleep, reclining in death, and the characteristic euphemism for sexual relations. Korean consistently distinguishes nuwotda ('reclined') from dongchimhaetda ('lay with sexually'), while Spanish separates acostarse from yacer con. The same root in Arabic (sakaba) means only 'to pour out,' a meaning surviving in one enigmatic occurrence at Job 38:37 about tilting heaven's water-jars. The Hifil adds tender domestic scenes of laying a child down, and the rare Hofal appears in Ezekiel's underworld tableaux where warriors 'are laid' among the slain.

senses.1: The fundamental Qal sense: lying down for rest, sleep, or repose. At 183 occurrences this dominates — Samuel lying in the temple (1 Sam 3:5, 9), the idiom 'lie down and rise up' bracketing daily life (Deut 6:7). Arabic ittaja'a ('to recline'), Spanish acostarse, and Korean nuwotda all converge on the basic posture of physical rest.
senses.2: The Qal euphemistic sense of sexual intercourse — 'to lie with' someone, always marked by prepositions 'im or 'et. Sixteen occurrences from Lot's daughters (Gen 19:33, 35) to the rape of Dinah (Gen 34:2) and legal casuistry (Deut 22:22–29). Korean dongchimhaetda and Arabic daja'a ma'a confirm the euphemistic idiom as a lexicalized sense.
senses.3: The Hifil causative: to lay someone down, typically in caretaking. The Shunammite woman laid Elisha's staff beside her dead son (2 Kgs 4:21), Solomon's mother placed one infant beside another (1 Kgs 3:20), Elijah laid the widow's son on his bed (1 Kgs 17:19). Arabic adja'a and Spanish acostar confirm seven occurrences of deliberate, tender placement.
senses.4: The Hofal passive-causative: to be laid down or placed in a reclining position. Used in Ezekiel's underworld oracles where slain warriors 'are laid' among the uncircumcised dead (Ezek 32:19, 32) and the Shunammite's son 'was laid' on Elisha's bed (2 Kgs 4:32). Arabic yudja'u confirms a state of having been placed by another's action.
senses.5: The Nifal and Pual passive stems denoting sexual violation — the passive counterpart to Sense 2 but with coercion. Isaiah 13:16 warns Babylon's women 'will be violated,' Zechariah 14:2 echoes the judgment, and Jeremiah 3:2 accuses Israel of roadside harlotry. Korean yok-boirira ('will be shamed sexually') and Arabic tudaja'na confirm violation semantics.
senses.6: A singular occurrence at Job 38:37 meaning 'pour out' or 'tilt over' — 'who can tilt heaven's water-jars?' This preserves the ancient Arabic cognate sakaba ('to pour out water or tears'), otherwise lost in Hebrew. Spanish volcar ('to overturn') confirms the liquid-discharge sense, a lexical fossil connecting postural semantics to pouring from a tilted vessel.

gloss_terse: To love; as participle: lover, friend, paramour; passive: beloved; also the abstract noun 'love' (ahavah)
gloss_readable: The Hebrew Bible's primary love verb spans from the tenderest human affection to the fiercest prophetic accusation. Jacob loved Rachel (Gen 29:18), the great commandment demands loving God with all one's heart (Deut 6:5), yet the same root in the Piel intensive becomes the prophets' weapon: Hosea and Jeremiah hurl me'ahavayikh ('your paramours') at faithless Israel. Arabic splits the field — muhibb for wholesome 'one who loves' versus 'ushshaq for illicit lovers. The passive participle yields 'beloved,' the favored wife of Deuteronomy 21. Spanish confirms the morphological distinctions: amar (verb), amante (lover), amada (beloved).

senses.1: The core Qal verbal sense: active loving — emotional attachment, devotion, and affection directed toward persons, God, or things. At 129 occurrences this is the verb's center: Jacob loved Rachel (Gen 29:18), 'love your neighbor as yourself' (Lev 19:18). Arabic ahabba, Spanish amar, French aimer, and Korean saranghada all render the basic verbal action.
senses.2: The Qal active participle used substantivally: a lover, friend, ally, or devotee. Fifty-one occurrences including 'those who love me' in the Decalogue promise (Exod 20:6) and 'the one who loves wisdom' (Prov 29:3). Arabic muhibb ('one who loves') and Spanish el-que-ama confirm the substantivized agent noun, yielding 'my friends/allies' with suffixes.
senses.3: The Piel intensive participle: paramour or illicit lover, concentrated in prophetic marriage-metaphor. Seventeen occurrences in Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Lamentations (1:2, 19) where Israel's idolatrous alliances are depicted as adultery. Arabic 'ushshaq ('passionate/illicit lovers') distinguishes these from the wholesome Qal 'friends' of Sense 2.
senses.4: The passive participle: the beloved, the cherished one — someone who is the object of love. Nine occurrences including the 'beloved wife' versus 'unloved wife' distinction (Deut 21:15–16), the eulogy of Saul and Jonathan as 'beloved and pleasant' (2 Sam 1:23). Arabic mahbub and Spanish amada confirm passive-resultative semantics.
senses.5: The abstract noun 'ahavah: the state or quality of love itself. Four occurrences where the noun functions independently: Jacob's years 'seemed like a few days because of his love' (Gen 29:20), 'a time to love and a time to hate' (Eccl 3:8). Arabic mahabbah and German Liebe (versus lieben) confirm the nominalization.
senses.6: A difficult singular occurrence at Hosea 4:18 where the text reads 'they love — give!' or 'her rulers dearly love shame.' Multilingual evidence diverges: English 'give,' Spanish 'Dan,' French 'le-en-lui' — suggesting textual corruption or an unusual elliptical construction. The economic domain assignment reflects emphasis on bribery or tribute rather than emotion.

gloss_terse: To judge, govern, vindicate, contend at law; as participle: judge (office-holder); Niphal: be judged, stand trial
gloss_readable: Shaphat is the legal and governmental verb of the Hebrew Bible — covering the full arc from courtroom adjudication to national governance to divine vindication of the oppressed. In the Judges period, the shofet was not merely an arbitrator but a charismatic military-political leader, a sense Arabic qada (spanning both 'judge' and 'rule') confirms. The same verb turns adversarial in the Niphal to mean 'enter into a lawsuit,' as when God challenges Israel to contend with Him (Isa 43:26). Spanish distinguishes juzgar (adjudicate) from gobernar (govern) and vindicar (vindicate), mapping the same fractures visible in the Hebrew evidence.

senses.1: The foundational Qal verbal action: judging, rendering verdicts, administering justice. Ninety-eight occurrences from Samuel judging Israel at Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah (1 Sam 7:16) to Solomon's prayer for judicial wisdom (1 Kgs 3:9). Arabic hakama, Spanish juzgar, French juger, and Korean simpanhada converge on forensic adjudication.
senses.2: The Qal active participle lexicalized as the substantive 'judge' (shofet/shoftim). Sixty-one occurrences spanning judicial appointment (Deut 16:18), the divine title 'Judge of all the earth' (Gen 18:25), and the era's named officeholders. Arabic al-qadi, Spanish el juez, and German der Richter confirm fully nominalized status.
senses.3: Qal forms with benefactive or vindicatory force: judging on behalf of, championing the oppressed. Sixteen occurrences including David's plea 'Judge me, O LORD' (Ps 7:8), 'Vindicate me, O God' (Ps 26:1), and Isaiah's call to 'judge the fatherless' (Isa 1:17). Arabic ihkum li ('judge for me') and Spanish juzgame confirm the pro-plaintiff orientation.
senses.4: Niphal and related forms of reciprocal judicial action: entering a lawsuit, contending at law, litigating. Thirteen occurrences including God's 'I will enter into judgment with you' (Ezek 20:35–36), the futility of contending with God (Job 9:15), and the fool's courtroom (Prov 29:9). Arabic haakama (Form III, 'to litigate') marks the shift from authority to adversarial engagement.
senses.5: Qal extended from judicial to political governance — ruling or leading a people in the pre-monarchic pattern. Eleven occurrences: 'give us a king to judge us' meaning 'to govern us' (1 Sam 8:5–6), Moses sitting all day 'judging' as executive (Exod 18:13). Arabic qada with governance connotation and the book of Judges confirm shaphat as the pre-monarchic term for leadership.
senses.6: The Niphal passive: to be judged, to stand trial, to undergo judgment. Five occurrences including 'let the nations be judged before you' (Ps 9:19), the assurance for the righteous (Ps 37:33), and the devastating 'when he is judged, let him come out guilty' (Ps 109:7). Arabic yudan and Korean simpan-batda confirm the passive voice.
